fatal_errors: The proposed oxygen-doping/TiO-precipitation intervention does not reconstruct the target comparison of CrFeTaVW with Ta-substituted CrFeTiVW using hybrid MD/MC, mechanical alloying, and spark-plasma sintering.
The response predicts mechanical strengthening at 1273 K, whereas the target outcomes concern phase constitution, segregation, and thermal diffusivity over 300–1000 K.
It does not evaluate thermal diffusivity, W/CuCrZr heat-transfer performance, or interfacial compatibility, so suitability as a heat-transfer interlayer is not established.

The cited TiO evidence is from a different NbMoTaWVTi alloy and does not demonstrate stable precipitation strengthening at 1273 K; E1 provides no support for TiO and instead reports severe high-temperature softening.
The claimed 30–40% strength increase and retained 30–40% ductility have no quantitative evidentiary basis.
explanation: The hypothesis is a scientifically conceivable oxide-precipitation-strengthening alternative, and its doped-versus-control experiment could test whether TiO forms and improves high-temperature strength. However, it has essentially no reconstruction agreement with the hidden study: the compositions, intervention, processing, simulations, mechanisms, baselines, measurements, and outcomes are different. Evidence E2 supports TiO-containing microstructures and precipitation strengthening only in another mechanically alloyed/SPS refractory alloy, without isolating oxygen addition or proving strength retention at 1273 K. The experiment also needs oxygen-dose controls, precipitate stability measurements before and after exposure, and thermal-diffusivity and W/alloy/CuCrZr interface tests. Its falsification rule partly confounds failure to produce TiO with falsification of TiO strengthening and uses an arbitrary 30–40% threshold.
